## Results

- Paired course-of-action comparison with common random numbers: support-by-fire wins 0.678 [0.658, 0.699] against maneuver at 0.649 [0.628, 0.670], 2,000 replications each, paired difference +0.029 [+0.009, +0.050]. Sharing random numbers halved the variance of the comparison
- Sobol sensitivity analysis: probability of kill at tank range dominates the outcome (total-order index 0.61-0.79), with a Gaussian-process metamodel at leave-one-out R2 0.75-0.86
- Kim-Nelson ranking and selection, history-matching calibration, and a 47-suite test harness that runs the engine, the estimators and the calibration in under 11 minutes
- Convergence testing showed the 25 m grid is not converged against 12.5 m, so the model is used to compare plans rather than to predict absolute probabilities

## The problem

Comparing courses of action with a stochastic combat model is only useful if the comparison is statistically honest (paired, interval-bounded, selection-bias-aware), the discretization is checked, and the parameters have a defined path from notional to calibrated.

## What I built

I built an entity engine that runs on OpenStreetMap, DEM or synthetic ground: detection hazard, multinomial-logit target choice, circular-normal hit probability, suppression, and Beta breakpoints, with named random substreams so two courses of action share random numbers. Around it I built the analysis toolkit: Wilson, delta and sup-t intervals, Kaplan-Meier and Aalen-Johansen for censored outcomes, Kim-Nelson ranking and selection, a Latin hypercube design with a stochastic-kriging Gaussian process and Saltelli-Jansen Sobol indices, and history matching with implausibility waves and a held-out terrain coverage check. An aggregate brigade engine is derived as a mean-field limit of the entity kill chain and bias-corrected against it.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## What it is for

Supports course-of-action analysis, which scheme of maneuver is better and with what confidence, and demonstrates the verification, validation and calibration process that Army analytic organizations apply to combat models.
:::

## Tools

Python, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn (GP), pandas, Streamlit, pydeck, Altair, OpenStreetMap / Overpass, AWS Terrain Tiles, pytest

[Parameters are notional. The model is verified against its specification, not validated against real engagements.]{.fine}
